Alpha scope and known limitations

What the 0.1.0a1 alpha does, what is in, preview or out, and the known limitations to read before relying on it.

DeveloperOperatorDecision-makerConceptBETA
PrerequisitesNone
Reviewed 2026-10-15 · 0.1.0a1 alpha

Release status (2026-10-15): 0.1.0a1 is the version prepared on main. The caliber-v0.1.0a1 tag and downloadable release assets have not been published. The capabilities below describe the current code and its CI proof; use Alpha install to build wheels from a checkout until the prerelease is available.

CALIBER 0.1.0a1 is an alpha. This page says what it does, what it does not do, and what to watch for, so you judge it against what it claims. It is the short version of the alpha gap analysis, which has the evidence and the reasoning.

What the alpha does#

A small team can self-host CALIBER from documented steps (Alpha install) and, through the web app or the Python SDK, do this with an audit trail and honest failure reporting:

  1. Author a prompt.
  2. Build a test set.
  3. Calibrate the prompt to get a candidate with evaluation evidence.
  4. Review the candidate and explicitly apply it to the live MLflow alias.
  5. See what is live and which job, dataset version and evaluation put it there.
  6. Roll it back.

The same loop works for a skill, a tool and a workflow (the extended tier), and, where an object store is configured, for building and querying a knowledge base.

Two things about the evidence. With the shipped defaults the language model and the evaluator are simulated: calibration runs and returns a candidate, but the scores are canned, and every screen, audit row and release record that carries them says so. Real evidence needs a real model and evaluator (Real LLM and evaluation). And the browser journey is proven in CI on every change, offline, on the simulated defaults.

Supported setups#

ItemAlpha support
DatabasePostgreSQL. SQLite works for evaluation and demos when MLflow uses its own, separate store.
MLflowA separate mlflow server (3.15 or later) over HTTP. Embedded --app-name caliber is not supported.
InstallRelease wheels with a native MLflow, or the Docker Compose stack.
Object storeNeeded only for knowledge bases and the object-store console.
Python3.10, 3.11 or 3.12.

What is in, preview, and out#

MaturityAreas
Core journeyPrompts, test sets, evaluations, calibration, review and Apply, projects and roles, access tokens, audit log, release timeline, readiness
Also in the alphaSkills, tools (trusted authors), workflows, knowledge bases and the object-store console
Preview (off by default)MCP servers and OpenAPI integrations (off by default; enable with CALIBER_FEATURE_INTEGRATIONS), cookbooks (off by default; enable with CALIBER_FEATURE_COOKBOOKS), the Aria assistant and plans (off by default; enable with CALIBER_FEATURE_ARIA). Marked "Preview" in the app once enabled
Record-only (off by default)Release-candidate signoff on the Releases page: it records a decision and deploys nothing (off by default; enable with CALIBER_FEATURE_RELEASE_CANDIDATES)
Experimental (off by default)Workspace releases: release evaluation has no executor in this build (off by default; enable with CALIBER_FEATURE_RELEASE_CANDIDATES)

The live board, the release timeline and release operations on the Releases page are core and always on. Only the release-candidate signoff and workspace releases are behind a flag.

Feature flags#

The areas above that the alpha does not stand behind are off by default and sit behind four server-side flags. A flag is read once at startup from the process environment, like the other CALIBER_* settings, so restart CALIBER after you change one. It is on for true, 1, yes or on (any case) and off for anything else, including unset.

Flag idVariableWhat it turns on
ariaCALIBER_FEATURE_ARIAThe Aria assistant and plans (preview): the /assistant/* and /aria/* routes, the Aria panel and the Plans page
integrationsCALIBER_FEATURE_INTEGRATIONSMCP servers and OpenAPI integrations (preview): the /mcp-servers* and /openapi-integrations* routes and their pages. While it is off, a workflow MCP node is reported as unavailable ("A registered MCP server that CALIBER can reach (needs CALIBER_FEATURE_INTEGRATIONS=true)")
cookbooksCALIBER_FEATURE_COOKBOOKSCookbooks (preview): the /cookbooks* routes and the Cookbooks page
release_candidatesCALIBER_FEATURE_RELEASE_CANDIDATESRelease-candidate signoff and workspace releases (record-only and experimental): the /releases/candidates*, /releases/report-jobs* and /projects/{id}/releases* routes and the candidate part of the Releases page

For example, to try Aria and the cookbooks:

export CALIBER_FEATURE_ARIA=true
export CALIBER_FEATURE_COOKBOOKS=true

Things to know before you turn one on:

  • Turning a flag on means you accept the behavior of that area. Preview areas may change or be removed without notice. A release-candidate signoff records a decision and deploys or rolls back nothing, and a workspace release evaluation stays queued because nothing in this build executes it. Enabling a flag does not move an area into the supported journey.
  • The areas depend on each other. The seventeen cookbooks build on other areas, so a lab can need more than CALIBER_FEATURE_COOKBOOKS: labs 12 to 15 need CALIBER_FEATURE_ARIA, lab 05 needs CALIBER_FEATURE_INTEGRATIONS, and lab 11 needs CALIBER_FEATURE_RELEASE_CANDIDATES. Each lab's README names the flags it needs.
  • Aria also backs a few helpers inside supported pages. The Ask Aria button, Describe it prompt drafting, the prompt Playground, test-case generation and test runs inside the prompt workspace, and the tool unit-test generator call the assistant, so with CALIBER_FEATURE_ARIA off they are hidden or show a "disabled in this deployment" notice. The core journey does not need them: build the test set by hand on the Test Sets page.
  • A disabled area answers 404. Every route of a disabled area returns HTTP 404 with the machine-readable reason_code feature_disabled, so a client can tell "this deployment has it off" from "no such record" (the body is shown below).
  • Feature detection. GET /capabilities returns a features object keyed by the four ids, each with enabled, env_var, label and stability, so a client reads the flags without provoking a 404. The web app does the same: it hides the navigation entries of a disabled area and shows a "disabled in this deployment" panel if you open one of its URLs directly.
  • The Docker stack passes the variables through. The four variables default to false there too; set them in the suite-root .env (see .env.example). See Alpha install.

A call to a route of a disabled area looks like this:

{
  "detail": "Cookbooks is disabled in this deployment. Set CALIBER_FEATURE_COOKBOOKS=true to enable it.",
  "status_code": 404,
  "reason_code": "feature_disabled"
}

Known limitations#

These are real and deliberate for the alpha. Read them before you rely on the product.

  • No trace-to-refinement automation. Nothing watches MLflow for flagged traces. There is no feedback poller and no "flag this trace" action in the app, and verifying an item in the queue does not start a job. Calibration starts from a prompt and a test set, which you create. Submitting feedback on a trace records an assessment in MLflow and an audit row, and does nothing else.
  • Traces and MLflow data are visible to every signed-in user. The observability pages and the trace and metric routes are not scoped to a project, so anyone who can sign in can read traces, including their inputs and outputs. Do not put sensitive data in traces on a shared alpha deployment.
  • Apply has no two-person rule. One person with the owner or editor role in the project can review and apply a candidate. The approval record is created at Apply time as the audit and rollback anchor, and it records who applied. It is not a second approver.
  • CSRF protection is off by default. CALIBER_CSRF_ENABLED defaults to false, on the assumption of a loopback or trusted-network deployment. Turn it on, and set a signing secret, before exposing CALIBER beyond that.
  • Simulated by default. The LLM and evaluator default to fake. The provider banner and the Settings page say so, and it cannot be dismissed while the evaluator or promoter is simulated.
  • SQLite needs a separate MLflow store. CALIBER and MLflow can share one SQLite file in development, and startup warns when they do, but only one writer wins at a time. Use PostgreSQL for anything shared.
  • The tool sandbox is a process boundary, not isolation. Tool code runs in a short-lived, environment-empty process with resource limits. Register tools only from authors you trust.
  • Knowledge bases need an S3-compatible bucket, the knowledge-local extra (torch and sentence-transformers) and a one-time embedding-model download. Without a reachable object store, creating one fails fast with a 503, and without the extra every embedding model is listed as unavailable. The default docker image installs knowledge but not knowledge-local, so it cannot build a knowledge base until you add it to CALIBER_INSTALL_EXTRAS. The storage and build path is tested against a real MinIO and PostgreSQL with simulated embeddings; no CI job exercises a real model.
  • Gate verdicts are not project-scoped. /gate-verdicts keys a verdict by a free-form string that names no artifact, so any operator can overwrite any verdict. It is advisory: no release or promotion decision reads it.
  • No HA, no performance targets, no SSO or MFA, no multi-tenant hosting.
  • Backups are documented, not rehearsed. See Backup and recovery.
  • No upgrade guarantees from earlier tags, and the packages are not on PyPI. Build wheels from a checkout until the prerelease assets are published.
  • Preview areas may change or be removed without notice. They are off by default; see Feature flags.
